title_original: In Oscar Contender ‘Ba’s Book,’ A Filmmaker Explores Her Father’s Remarkable Past, Bringing Them Closer Together – For The Love Of Docs

blocks.text: Of the 190 feature documentaries to qualify for Academy Award consideration this year, one Oscar contender stands out for its unique exploration of family dynamics and the legacy of the Vietnam War.

Canadian filmmaker Ashley Da-Lê Duong directed Ba’s Book , a film whose title refers to a memoir written by her father, Anh Duong, in which he described his experience growing up during the catastrophic conflict between Communist North Vietnam and the U.S.-allied South Vietnam. Ba’s Book screened Tuesday night as part of Deadline’s For the Love of Docs virtual event series.

blocks.text: Ashley’s father had sent her a draft of his memoir while she was visiting Vietnam. He had written it fearing that Ashley traveling there, and meeting members of his family he had left behind when he settled in Canada, might given her a misimpression about his past.
Watch on Deadline

blocks.alt: Anh Duong (center) and director Ashley Da-Lê Duong in 'Ba's Book.' At left is an actor cast in reenactments of Anh's life.
blocks.caption: Anh Duong (center) and director Ashley Da-Lê Duong in ‘Ba’s Book.’ At left is an actor cast in reenactments of Anh’s life. Intuitive Pictures/Da-Lê Films

blocks.text: “After I received my dad’s manuscript, I knew right away that this is an amazing story,” she said during a panel discussion after the screening. “It took me a long time though, a few years, before I really figured out how I wanted to do it [as a film], because I needed to make sure my relationship with my father was at a point where it was strong enough.”

In his book, Anh not only recounted near-death experiences as war raged around him, but he revealed that as a young man he had been able to leave Vietnam for Tehran, after receiving a scholarship to study engineering there in 1979. Within a few months, Anh was plunged into the middle of the Islamic Revolution. That was all news to Ashley. Up to that point, her father’s past and perhaps the man himself, had been a mystery to her.

“Before he wrote his memoir, he never even mentioned to me he went to Iran, let alone lived there for five years. So, the level of not telling me the stories was very high,” Ashley noted. “I would joke that he was like the Forrest Gump of Asia. He’s just been in all these pivotal moments of history.”
As to family history – his relationship with his siblings and his mom who did not necessarily share his viewpoint on the war and Vietnamese politics – Anh had written relatively little.

“I also didn’t want to just tell his story [in the film] because my dad has told his story through his book,” she commented. “I wanted to expand on it and include the perspectives of my relatives and myself and really see how the effects of war and how a family moves forward 50 years after the Vietnam War.”

blocks.alt: Anh Duong (right) with an actor portraying him in 'Ba's Book.'
blocks.caption: Anh Duong (right) with an actor portraying him in ‘Ba’s Book.’ Intuitive Pictures/Da-Lê Films

blocks.text: Ashley took the bold approach of casting actors to portray important moments from her father’s life. As she filmed those scenes, her relatives were on set, observing along with her father, who had traveled from Canada to witness her reenact his youth.

“When I saw the movie, someone [playing] me in the movie, [I reacted], ‘Oh, what? It’s me!’” Anh said. “So, I’m very happy that she made a film about me… Of course, at first we have a lot of disagreements [about how things would be filmed], but after we have a long talk, we come up with what we can tell and what not tell.”

“One thing that I learned while making it was that my dad wasn’t going to give me exactly what I wanted. He was going to do what he wanted and say what he wanted,” Ashley noted. “And there’s a choice you need to make as a documentary filmmaker. You can try to massage it so it’s the way you want, or you can just show those tensions. For example, in one of the moments where he’s running down into the bomb shelter, he was insisting that I make it two scenes, even though for me, narratively, they didn’t make sense as two scenes. But it was something that I felt like I actually had to listen to the reason why he was telling me that.”

Ashley continued, “And then he told me about how people he knew died during that first instance, so I can’t combine it with another instance. And there were these important reasons why. And listening to my dad’s just telling [and] me learning to listen to him was I think one of the biggest parts of the process of filming.”
Oscar-nominated producer Ina Fichman ( Fire of Love ) saw the value in Ashley’s cinematic approach.

“I’m a big fan of films like Stories We Tell and Joshua Oppenheimer’s films and felt, wow, this is really interesting to somehow put your family — both your extended family and your father — into this really unique situation of telling a story and recalling memory by ‘reenacting.’ And I use that word very loosely because in the doc space, reenactments can mean many, many things.”

Fichman added, “As a documentary producer, I’m always looking for projects that push the boundaries. And this was an ambitious idea. This was not an easy idea. How do you go to Vietnam and work with non-professional actors and Ashley’s family — who at that point she didn’t know very well — and bring her father to actually recollect things that were very difficult? And what was extraordinary is that it worked.”
Ba’s Book shows a novel way to achieve a breakthrough in family communication, one that may resonate with people of any background.

“Every family has secrets. And I’ve met many children of Holocaust survivors whose parents have never spoken to them about what they’ve gone through. And I think the impact, not just on the relationship within the family, but on each individual is very profound,” Fichman observed. “And I’m hoping this film will help us understand how important that is, that it is not easy, but it’s game changing. And look at Ashley and her father’s relationship. It really transformed it. So, I think that’s what I’m hoping that audiences will take away, that this isn’t just a film about Vietnam. It’s a film about how we live. We all live trauma in our lives, in our past and in our present. And having the ability to go there is really meaningful and game changing.”
